extracted.intended_audience: picture-book authors and illustrators (and adults who read picture books aloud: librarians, teachers, parents)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on designing a picture book specifically to be funny when read aloud in storytime: establishing premise, building a game/rules, aligning text and visuals, pacing page-turns, and shaping both child and adult reactions. Focus is on author/illustrator choices that produce audible laughs and sustain tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for read-aloud / portable comedy routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the book a portable comedy routine that elicits audible reactions from a group of kids and gives the adult reader the feeling of getting laughs at storytime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly aimed to 'create, essentially, a portable comedy routine' so every page can elicit an audible reaction—even from 'rowdy back-of-the-gym kids.' Treat the book as a performative object, not just a printed story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the premise quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Open decisively so readers immediately understand the conceit (e.g., first spread: 'This book is from the future. Lots of things are different here in the future').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first pages should rapidly introduce the point of view and root it (the author notes the importance of the word 'here' to root the point of view in the future). Make the opening declarative and simple so the game can begin right away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce and reinforce a clear game/rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Set a simple rule (here: names of things have been swapped) and reinforce it early so the audience understands the pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: second spread introduces the swapping rule and then reinforces the pattern so readers 'think we have a grip on how the future works.' Early reinforcement establishes the game's logic and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite audience participation (fill-in-the-blank)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design spreads that invite children to answer aloud before the page turn (third spread invites the audience to use what they learned to fill in a blank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prompts that encourage vocal responses; rely on timing (kids usually answer on the recto before you turn the page) to build participatory laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surprise/subversion after building expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: After lulling readers into a pattern, subvert their guess on the verso so the audience is surprised and discovers more rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn the page to reveal that 'our guess is wrong'—the joke works by undermining assumptions and adding layers, e.g., the recto sets an expectation and the verso surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror textual patterns with visual rules and ease them in
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce visual motifs gradually to echo the book's textual rules (e.g., progression from black text to planet to repeated circles to full-bleed scene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual rhythm (same-size circles in same place, then vignettes, then full bleed) lulls readers into accepting patterns. The visuals should teach the same 'game' as the text so readers learn both mechanics together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use page-turns, pacing, and 'trapdoor' moments to land jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure spreads and page turns (including abrupt visual shifts like black page with white text) to create the feeling of hitting a wall or a trapdoor that enhances the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recto/verso relationships carefully; use stark shifts (e.g., black page/white text) as comedic beats. The interview calls this feeling 'hitting a wall, or a trapdoor opening,' which is what the joke is doing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the narrator and delivery deadpan / play it straight
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the narrator (and often the illustrations) report the absurdities as if they are normal—this straight delivery heightens the comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mac: 'the narrator from the future thinks this stuff is all normal' and Shawn: 'I get to play the straight man next to Mac.' Keep tone flat and authoritative so the contrast with nonsense reads as funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give nonsense weight with authoritative design cues (typography/labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use visual treatments—like DYMO label-maker typography—so made-up or swapped words read as authoritative and therefore funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels on objects make ridiculous words 'feel authoritative.' The interview warns that arbitrary nonsense can lose tension unless framed—labels, a familiar typographic treatment, or placement on the object provide that frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familiar artifacts to ground absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor invented conventions with recognizable, cozy artifacts (e.g., a vintage DYMO label maker) to make absurd content believable and funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shawn used a real vintage Dymo to make labels 'cozy or quotidian,' which helps lull readers into comfort before the joke turns. Authentic props increase credibility and comic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read visual treatments flat to enhance the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the funny word look and be read flat (treatment makes you read them flat), which increases humor by contrast with the word's absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jon: the labels 'are the funny word, but the treatment makes you read them flat, which makes them even funnier.' Design type and placement so performance reads dry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance looseness and restraint in illustration style ('loose without wacky')
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for an illustration approach that feels loose but not wacky—so things feel fresh but not chaotic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shawn: 'I used a medium I have never used before so everything is still loose without looking wacky.' The goal is 'loose without wacky' to preserve control and comedic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign a clear visual role (straight man vs comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use illustration choices to play straight man to the text's comic voice; visual restraint can be the straight response to verbal absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shawn describes being the straight man visually next to Mac's text; let images provide calm/authority while text provides the nonsense punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect both child and adult reader experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Take care of the children in the audience and the adult reading out loud—make the book satisfying and playable for both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mac: 'We really wanted to take good care of both the audience and the adult reading this book out loud.' Build moments that reward kid participation and make the adult feel clever and funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalate pacing and risk thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Start carefully to teach the rules and then increase the riskiness of pacing and jokes so tension rises but ultimately pays off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jon compares the arc to a tightrope: you 'take these first steps so carefully, and then you start to dance up there'—the pacing should get riskier, but crafted so it doesn't 'fall on your face.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition and motifs to build rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on repeated motifs (labels, circle compositions, placement) to create a rhythm readers accept before you subvert it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circles in the same size and place, repeated label placements, and consistent visual grammar help lull the reader into predictability that the book can later upend for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for diverse storytime conditions (including rowdy groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose jokes and visual beats so they work across different audiences, including 'rowdy back-of-the-gym kids.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jon notes every page is designed to elicit an audible reaction even from disruptive audiences—favor bold, immediate beats over subtle, easily-missed cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary nonsense without a framing device
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't rely on gratuitous nonsense words; unless they are framed (e.g., by labels or authority) children will think 'now you’re just saying whatever' and the tension falls away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: inventing nonsense that feels untethered. Fix: provide a framing device (labels, narrator authority, consistent rule) so absurd language retains comedic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real materials/props for authenticity and design decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate real objects (e.g., an actual vintage DYMO) during design to inform visual choices and authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shawn bought a vintage Dymo on eBay and used it as a model—the tangible weight and look contributed to the idea that labels feel authoritative and funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let layout and sequencing serve the joke (recto/verso mechanics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan spreads so the recto can set up audience expectation and the verso can overturn it; visual/typographic choices should support that mechanic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interview details the specific spread progression (black text; circle earth; matching circles; vignettes; full bleed) as an example of sequencing that teaches the reader how to read the joke and then subverts it.
